steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Pacific Software: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 5 clients), $2,100 from Barclays, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,880/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Great Lakes, 2019–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — I can walk through this and tell you how these items are generally treated for U.S. federal income tax, what’s likely best for you, and which forms you’ll need. A few clarifying questions are at the end so I can give more precise numbers if you want.

Short summary / bottom line
- Your photography income will be reported as self‑employment income (Schedule C) and is subject to income tax and self‑employment (SE) tax. You can deduct ordinary & necessary business expenses against that income.
- The home‑office deduction is available for the exclusive 120 sq ft used for the photography business. Using actual expenses (Form 8829) will give a much larger deduction than the simplified method in your case.
- Charitable gift ($1,500) is deductible only if you itemize. With the information provided, the standard deduction will almost certainly be larger than your itemized deductions, so you’ll likely take the standard deduction.
- Student‑loan interest is an “above‑the‑line” adjustment (up to $2,500) if you qualify (phaseouts apply based on MAGI).
- Unreimbursed employee expenses for a W‑2 job are not deductible under current law; if those $1,050 are business expenses for the photography business, report them on Schedule C.

Quick numbers (estimates from what you gave)
- Gross amounts: W‑2 $68,200 + photography $16,300 + interest $2,100 + Merrill Edge $420 = $87,020 total gross income before business expense adjustments.
- Rent: $1,880/month = $22,560/year. Home office share = 120/720 = 16.6667%.
  - Actual‑expense home office deduction (your rent portion) = 22,560 × 16.6667% = $3,760.
  - Simplified method = $5 × 120 = $600.
  So actual method gives $3,760 — recommend actual method (Form 8829) because it’s larger.

What you can (generally) deduct
- Photography business (Schedule C):
  - Business expenses (equipment, supplies, business travel, advertising, insurance, website fees, etc.).
  - Home office: either Form 8829 (actual expenses allocated by square footage) or the simplified $5/sq‑ft method (max 300 sq ft). Based on your rent, actual method yields a bigger deduction ($3,760 vs $600).
  - If the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” are business expenses for the photography work, include them on Schedule C.
  - Self‑employment tax: you’ll pay SE tax (Social Security + Medicare) on net self‑employment earnings; half of the SE tax is deductible on Schedule 1 as an adjustment to income.
- Student‑loan interest:
  - Up to $2,500 may be deductible as an adjustment to income (Schedule 1) if you paid interest in the tax year and your MAGI is below the phaseout threshold. You mentioned $5,100 — I need to confirm what year(s) those payments were made (only interest paid in the tax year you are filing for is deductible, and you should receive Form 1098‑E for interest paid in the tax year).
- Charitable gift:
  - $1,500 to Salvation Army is an itemized deduction (Schedule A) — only useful if your itemized total exceeds the standard deduction.
- Investment/bank interest:
  - Report Barclays 1099‑INT and Merrill Edge amounts (1099‑INT / 1099‑DIV / 1099‑B) on your Form 1040.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses for W‑2 work:
  - NOT deductible for most employees under current law. (They were suspended by the TCJA through at least 2025.)

Will you itemize or take the standard deduction?
- Given only $1,500 in charitable donations and no mortgage interest or big state tax deductions (you live in Texas), your itemized deductions are likely well below the standard deduction for a single filer. So you will almost certainly take the standard deduction.
- If you have other deductible items you didn’t list (large medical expenses, mortgage interest, big charitable gifts, or other qualifying itemized amounts), that could change the decision. Let me know if there are more items.

Forms you’ll likely need
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule 1 — additional income (e.g., adjustments) and adjustments (student loan interest, half of SE tax, etc.).
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report photography gross receipts ($16,300) and business expenses (including home office share from Form 8829).
- Schedule SE — calculate self‑employment tax.
- Form 8829 — if you choose the actual home office method (prorated rent and other home expenses). If you use the simplified method, you don’t file 8829 — you enter the simplified deduction on Schedule C.
- Schedule A — only if you itemize (to claim the $1,500 charitable gift). If you take the standard deduction, you don’t file Schedule A.
- Form 1098‑E — student loan interest statement you should receive from Great Lakes if you paid interest during the year (you need this to claim the adjustment).
- 1099‑NEC / 1099‑MISC — if you received for photography work; if not, you still report the income.
- 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, 1099‑B — from Barclays / Merrill Edge for interest/dividends/transactions.
- State return — none for Texas (no state income tax).

Other important notes and steps
- Keep good records: invoices, client payments, receipts for supplies/equipment, rent/lease proof, utility bills, mileage logs if you claim vehicle business use, and the donation receipt for Salvation Army.
- Estimated tax: because you have self‑employment income, you may owe quarterly estimated taxes. If you expect to owe $1,000+ when you file, you should have been making estimated payments during the year (Form 1040‑ES). You’ll also owe SE tax in addition to income tax on self‑employment net earnings.
- Student loan interest phaseout: the deduction phases out at higher MAGI levels. With the rough gross income shown (~$87k before business deductions), you may be near or inside the phaseout range. I’ll need exact MAGI (after adjustments) or the tax year’s phaseout thresholds to confirm eligibility.
- If the home office is used exclusively and regularly for the photography business, it is eligible. If you use it for any personal purpose, the exclusive‑use requirement is not met and the deduction is disallowed.
- If the $1,050 unreimbursed is for W‑2 job expenses, you cannot deduct it. If it was for the photography business, include it on Schedule C.

What I need from you to run more exact calculations / recommendations
- Confirm the tax year you’re filing for (I assume 2024).
- Confirm whether the $16,300 is gross receipts from your photography business (and whether that included any business expenses already subtracted).
- Confirm whether the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” are for photography (self‑employment) or for your W‑2 job.
- Clarify the student loan interest: did you actually pay $5,100 in interest during the tax year you’re filing for, or is that a cumulative figure from 2019–2021? Do you have Form 1098‑E for the tax year?
- Do you have any other deductible items (mortgage interest, large medical expenses, unreimbursed losses, large charitable contributions, casualty losses, etc.)?

Would you like me to:
- do a rough calculation of taxable income, self‑employment tax, and estimated federal tax owed using the numbers above (I can show line‑by‑line estimates), or
- prepare a checklist of documents to gather for filing, or
- draft the language for a Schedule C summary and Form 8829 entries you (or your preparer) can use?

I’m happy to run numbers once you confirm the clarifying details. Also note I’m giving general guidance — if your situation is complex or you want exact tax‑minimization strategies, a CPA/tax preparer can give definitive, up‑to‑date answers and prepare your forms.
